teaser: In 1977 this face was the emblem of a whole continent's festival. The original stayed locked in a museum.
review_notes:
FESTAC '77 emblem was based on the sister mask in the British Museum, not the Met's; the loan refusal and Erhabor Emokpae's replica are widely reported.
Identification with Idia, mother of Oba Esigie, is the traditional and scholarly consensus, not documented by inscription.
Height 23.8 cm per the Met.
In this photo the pupil inlay looks dark in one eye and paler in the other: please check the wording of that spot.
The metal wire around the lower collar looks like a mount or repair; not commented on.
Mask said to have been found in a chest in the Oba's bedchamber in 1897: reported for the ivory masks, please verify.
Met credit line: gift of Nelson A. Rockefeller, 1972.

lesson.text: Lagos, 1977. Nigeria hosts FESTAC, a giant festival of Black and African culture, and its emblem is everywhere: on posters, stamps, banknotes, T-shirts. The emblem is this face. Or rather its twin, a sister mask kept in the British Museum, which refused to lend it. A Nigerian sculptor had to carve a replica.

The mask you are looking at is the one in New York. Both were made in the same court around 1520, in the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria. Do not confuse it with the modern country of Benin, which lies further west.

It is small: 23.8 centimeters, about 9 inches, the size of an open hand. And it is not a mask to cover a face. It is a pendant, carved from elephant ivory and thin as a shell, made to be worn by one person only: the king, called the Oba.

The face is thought to be Idia, mother of Oba Esigie. When Esigie's brother fought him for the throne, and then a neighboring kingdom invaded, Idia is said to have raised an army and advised her son through both wars. He won, and he thanked her in a way no woman in Benin had been thanked before.
Esigie created a new title for his mother: Iyoba, Queen Mother, with her own palace and court. This pendant is the portrait of a woman who held real political power.
Her calm face is framed by a kind of openwork crown. From far away it reads as lace. It is actually a row of tiny carved creatures, and two different kinds alternate.
Hidden in the crown are small human heads with hats and long hair. Tap one.

spots.title: A Portuguese trader
spots.text: A tiny bearded head with a brimmed hat and straight hair: a Portuguese man. Between each of these heads curls a mudfish, a fish able to survive both in water and on land.

lesson.text: Why crown an African queen with Europeans? Portuguese ships had reached Benin in the 1480s. They came from the sea, and they brought brass, coral and cloth in exchange for pepper, ivory and, soon, enslaved people. For the court, they were a sign of the Oba's wealth and reach.

The mudfish carries a second message. A creature at home in two worlds is a good symbol for a king who was seen as partly human and partly divine. Even the material speaks: white ivory was linked to Olokun, god of the sea and of riches.
Elephant ivory was a royal monopoly in Benin. When a hunter killed an elephant, one tusk went to the Oba by right, and he could choose to buy the other.

lesson.title: Not only ivory
lesson.text: The carver added other materials to the face, and four practical details. Three stops.

spots.title: Two dark bars
spots.text: Two strips of iron are set into the forehead, now rusted brown. They stand for scarification marks, patterns cut into the skin.

spots.title: The gaze
spots.text: The pupils and the rims of the eyes were inlaid with iron too. Here the dark metal still gives the eye a sharp, steady stare, with the lids lowered just a little.

spots.title: A lug
spots.text: This small carved block, repeated on the other side and again below each ear, is a loop for a cord. Four of them let the pendant be tied on.

lesson.text: Iron mattered as much as ivory. In Benin thought, the metal held a force that made things happen. Setting it into the forehead and eyes charged the portrait with power, and it gave Idia's face that slightly unsettling contrast of cream and black.

The Oba wore the pendant during ceremonies, probably at his hip, and likely in the yearly rites honoring his mother. Imagine it moving with him, the ivory catching the light against red coral beads and cloth.

In 1897 a British military expedition captured Benin City, burned much of the palace and carried off thousands of brass and ivory works. This mask was found in a chest in the Oba's bedchamber, along with its sister now in the British Museum.

It passed through British hands, then was bought by the American collector Nelson Rockefeller, who gave it to the Metropolitan Museum in 1972. Many works taken in 1897 have since been returned to Nigeria by other museums. The two ivory masks have not.

spots.title: The hair
spots.text: Hundreds of tiny drilled rings in neat rows. They show a cap of tight curls, or a net of beads. Each one was cut by hand.

spots.title: The mouth
spots.text: Full lips, closed and level. No smile, no frown: the calm of someone used to being obeyed.

spots.title: The nose
spots.text: Smooth, rounded, softly modeled. The carver balanced an ideal of beauty with the feeling of a real person.

spots.title: The collar
spots.text: Under the chin, another openwork band: a row of bearded Portuguese heads again, side by side like a ruff.

spots.title: Fine cracks
spots.text: A web of hairline cracks runs through the surface. Ivory dries and splits with age. This piece is about five hundred years old.

lesson.text: So the FESTAC emblem was the right choice, and a painful one. A face made to honor a mother's loyalty became, four and a half centuries later, the image of a continent asking for its own history back.

quiz.question: How was this object worn?
options: Over the face, by a dancer
As a pendant, by the king
On a necklace, by the Queen Mother herself
quiz.explanation: It is a pendant made for the Oba, not a face mask.

quiz.question: Which two creatures alternate in the crown?
quiz.explanation: Tiny Portuguese heads and mudfish alternate along the top.

quiz.question: What are the two dark bars on the forehead made of?
quiz.explanation: They are iron inlays standing for scarification marks.

quiz.question: What title did Oba Esigie create for his mother Idia?
Why did the mudfish suit a king?
options: It was the most expensive fish
It only lives in royal ponds
It lives both in water and on land, like a ruler between two worlds
quiz.explanation: The Oba was seen as partly human, partly divine.

quiz.question: What happened in 1897?
options: A British expedition looted Benin City
quiz.explanation: British troops captured the city and took thousands of works.

facts.text: The Kingdom of Benin was located in what is now Nigeria.
facts.explanation: Benin City is in southern Nigeria, not in the modern Republic of Benin.

facts.text: The mask is about as tall as a person.
facts.explanation: It is only 23.8 cm, about 9 inches.

facts.text: The British Museum lent its sister mask to Nigeria for the 1977 festival.
facts.explanation: The loan was refused, and a Nigerian sculptor carved a replica.
